win the game.)

> you are coming from another game (especially M:tG), it's just not appealing.
> You are killing yourself just so you can play? On the surface, it just doesn't
> make sense.

OK, this is the part I challenge. I suppose there's no accounting for taste and I
wouldn't dispute your word about it. But I just can't see why it would be
unappealing or nonsensical in any way, shape, or form. I've never heard any
newbies mention that this thing in particular bothered them nor would I ever
expect to. If you have, I would tend to write it off as either a weird anomaly
you've experience or something in what's being communicated to you that you're
failing to reflect accurately in your post. For instance, the _real_ frustration
your newbies may be encountering is losing against more experienced players which
they experience as a feeling of "damned-if-you-do-damned-if-you-don't" because
they somehow always find themselves caught between insufficient resources and an
insufficient buffer of pool to prevent a sudden rush of bleeding from ousting
them. If so, the problem is a very common one: they're losing a lot while
learning the strategies and tactics that allow them to balance pool and resources.
It just turns out that some form of pool gain is one of the key strategies in
managing one's pool. If it didn't exist, veteran players wouldn't be able to use
it either, thus it wouldn't be as much of a frustration for newer players.

Fred

I'd like to chime in with anecdotal evidence that you're right... When my
friends and I first started playing Jyhad, we *were* confused with the "life =
mana" mechanic in the game. Coming directly from Magic at the time, we saw
life and mana both as things you wanted to maximize, and the person that
effectively maximized both was going a long way towards winning the game.

In Jyhad, the amount you could spend on effects was very regimented (or so we
saw when we started). You had essentially 4 mana per turn, but each one you
used would cost life. So, in a way, it seemed like it would be better to not
bring out any vampires, as you would last longer that way. If you went for
bringing out 5 vampires (which seemed like a small amount of creatures to be
controlling, after the Goblin and Merfolk decks we had just finished playing
with), you were practically dead. You were just waiting for anyone with a
modicum of stealth to come over, bleed you for 2, and oust you. All those
creatures you controlled, and they didn't save you at all - they just made you
die faster.

Eventually, we went to 40 pool games, so that you could have enough pool to
bring out some reasonable number of creatures to see the interplay between
them. We felt that you should definitely be able to afford at least one 10-cap
, and 4 to 6 other vampires. We did this, and games lasted *hours* and
*hours*. So we quit the game for a while because it took too long.

When we came back to it a couple of months later, we ditched the 40-pool rule
and started playing "Anarch" (weenie) decks. From there, the metagame evolved
in ways which you are probably all aware.

But yeah, that's the story of the painful transition from "The Dark"-era Magic
to Jyhad. Granted, we are all wiser now (well, not all... some of us quit this
game), and know that you should never use the word "mana" or "creature" when
talking about Jyhad. ;)

sure Second and Fifth Traditions merited changing and, in any circumstances, I
mourn for yet two more cards that don't do what they do on the old versions -
assuming this rumor is true. But I do look forward to playing the game without
the wholesale refilling of minions with the old Fifth Tradition.

There are other ways to take care of weeny bleed. In fact, one of the main types
of weeny bleed may be taking a major hit if the other rumor about Majesty is true.
Weeny presence minions can less afford to play a blood every combat than anyone
else. And offensive combat, in some form or another (whether rush, intercept,
bleed and bruise, or whatever) should be more prevalent with presence S:CE being
harder to make work. So if you're convinced Minion Tap/Fifth Tradition is the
only way large minions can survive weeny bleed, I still think things may not be
so bad.

"life =
> > mana" mechanic in the game. Coming directly from Magic at the time, we saw
> > life and mana both as things you wanted to maximize, and the person that
> > effectively maximized both was going a long way towards winning the game.
>
> Confused, I'll buy. But could you explain why you would see that as a bad
> thing, as Sorrow is suggesting? After all, the rule is the same for
everyone.
> Everyone has to solve the same problem.
>

I'd like to postulate that confusion equals "bad" for starting players.
Granted, once you learn a game and understand that this mechanic is a decision
about spending pool in order to protect your pool, and one which everyone has
to find a way to deal with, well... then it ceases to be confusing and becomes
interesting. It's a part of the game. One way to explain this to people is to
show that you can use your minions to gain pool back. Thus, it's a sort of
investment, and most people understand investments.

Note, I don't think that the changes to blood gain that have so far been
"revealed" are a bad thing. But, I do see Sorrow's point. I don't think that
the pool investment mechanic in the game is a bad thing, but until you realize
that it's an investment, it can be confusing. Especially when considering how
you will best spend your pool. It's tough to go about solving a problem until
you have a handle on exactly what problem you're solving, and showing people
that there are ways to gain back pool goes at a least a little ways toward
explaining the problem.

> they see as a defect of the game (it doesn't matter that *you* don't see it as
> a defect). The way I did that was to show them bloat. Now, I can't really even
> do that anymore.

I guess what I was trying to get at was what was actually _bad_ about it. Granted,
there's always just arbitrary taste: "I don't like that in a game, so I'm not
going to play that game." That's fine. It's somewhat arbitrary but a lot of
people have certain things like that - including me.

But when you responded to this thread, you seemed to infer that it's a common,
widespread thing, which is what I can't understand. A game that takes more time
than a person likes to spend on games is something that might be common and
understandable to dislike. (As might a game that's too short, for that matter.)
A game like Magic where a spate of bad luck (e.g. drawing no land) will negate
any chance of winning the game, no matter how clever your deck, is something
that might be common and understandable to dislike. But there's nothing about
spending pool to gain resources to win the game that seems inherently "bad" to
me. It's just arbitrary to view it as "bad".

Fred

>So maybe the shift away from pool

One alternative option:

- Due to a perceived inability to gain pool as easily as previously,
decks will become more defensive

- As a result, more players will include Telepathic Counter, Deflection
and so on

- What pool gain there is will be seen as much more important. Combined
with a greater level of defence, this could create a greater
differential in general pool totals from current levels, when
defence is included (that is, even with a smaller total pool,
more bleed will be needed to break down defences)

- Games, overall, will take longer, as a result

I can see a metagame working this way, as well as the faster option.

My apologies if suggesting that some players, and thus affecting some
groups, which had relied on Fifth Tradition bloating for uber-pool gain
might go onto more defensive lines to compensate, doesn't meet with your
approval. Such reactions do happen, as new deck styles are explored, or
a ruling is issued, or whatever. Some players see a certain card as
being utterly whack, and so regard it as a much more powerful situation
than it really is - current example, Rotschreck. There are myriad
defences to it (and it's notable that the Rules Team 'added' another
one, using common disciplines[0]), yet players still perceive it as
being extremely powerful.

You may not view it as that. I may not view it as that. There are,
however, many players whose reactions and expectations regarding certain
cards and certain effects differs quite wildly from my own.

It can be quite enlightening (or less so) to listen to inexperienced
players whose views of cards are wildly different. I recall a gentleman
trying to sell the virtues of Blood Puppy to me.

Anyway, perception is nine tenths of the law. Just ask David Tatu.
